AGO.text: Mbanza Kongo, on a plateau at 570 m, was the capital of the Kingdom of Kongo, one of the largest states in Southern Africa from the 14th to the 19th century.

BDI.text: Near Gitega, in central Burundi, lie the southernmost source of the Nile and the spectacular Kagera Falls.

BEN.text: From 1625 to 1900, twelve kings ruled the Kingdom of Abomey. Almost all of them built their palaces inside the same earthen-walled enclosure.

BFA.text: The Loropeni ruins, with their imposing stone walls, are at least 1,000 years old. They recall the gold trade across the Sahara.

BWA.text: In Botswana, the Tsodilo Hills in the Kalahari Desert hold over 4,500 paintings in just 10 km². They are called the "Louvre of the Desert".

CAF.text: Sangha Trinational joins three neighbouring national parks of about 750,000 hectares, home to forest elephants and gorillas.

CIV.text: Taï National Park protects one of the last large pieces of primary tropical forest in West Africa, home to the pygmy hippopotamus and 11 species of monkeys.

CMR.text: Cameroon's Dja Faunal Reserve is almost surrounded by the Dja River and shelters 107 mammal species, including many primates.

COD.text: In the north-east, the Okapi Wildlife Reserve covers one-fifth of the Ituri forest, a refuge of the okapi, the "forest giraffe".

COG.text: The Equator crosses the Republic of the Congo, just north of the town of Liranga. Brazzaville is a major port on the Congo River.

COM.text: On Grande Comore island, Karthala is an active volcano of 2,361 m, the highest point in the Comoros.

CPV.text: Cidade Velha, on the island of Santiago, was called Ribeira Grande. You can still see two churches, a royal fortress and part of the original street layout.

DJI.text: Lake Assal, a salt lake in Djibouti, lies 155 m below sea level: it is the lowest point in Africa.

DZA.text: In Tassili n'Ajjer, in the Sahara, more than 15,000 prehistoric drawings and engravings decorate eroded sandstone shaped into "rock forests".

EGY.text: The pyramid fields from Giza to Dahshur surround Memphis, capital of the Old Kingdom. In ancient times, the site was counted among the Seven Wonders of the World.

ERI.text: Asmara, the capital of Eritrea, stands at over 2,000 m above sea level and is famous for its modernist architecture.

ETH.text: At Lalibela, in the heart of Ethiopia, eleven medieval churches were carved out of living rock in a mountainous region.

GAB.text: In Lopé-Okanda, rainforest and savannah meet, and the rocks carry about 1,800 prehistoric carvings.

GHA.text: Near Kumasi, the traditional Asante buildings, made of earth, wood and straw, are the last remains of the great Asante civilization of the 18th century.

GIN.text: Mount Nimba, on the border of Guinea, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire, shelters the viviparous toad and chimpanzees that use stones as tools.

GMB.text: Along the River Gambia, over 1,000 monuments, including circles of laterite pillars, form a sacred landscape created over more than 1,500 years.

GNB.text: In Guinea-Bissau, tides reach up to 100 km inland. Their brackish water is used to irrigate rice paddies called bolanhas.

GNQ.text: On Bioko island, Basile Peak is an extinct volcano rising to 3,008 m. The island also has crater lakes.

KEN.text: Lake Turkana in Kenya is the largest desert lake in the world. It is nicknamed the "Jade Sea" for its beautiful colour.

LBR.text: In Liberia, the Vai people invented their own alphabet, a script created right there.

LBY.text: Cyrene, founded by Greeks from the island of Thera, stayed a great capital until the earthquake of 365. A thousand years of history is written into its ruins.

LSO.text: In Lesotho, Sehlabathebe National Park shelters the Maloti minnow, a rare fish found only in this park.

MAR.text: Ait-Ben-Haddou, near Ouarzazate, is a ksar: earthen houses crowded together behind high walls reinforced by corner towers.

MDG.text: In Madagascar, the Bemaraha tsingy form a "forest of sharp stones": limestone pinnacles up to 100 metres high, like cathedrals.

MLI.text: In Djenné, nearly 2,000 traditional houses have survived. They are built on mounds called toguere to protect them from seasonal floods.

MOZ.text: In Mozambique, Chopi orchestras bring together five to thirty wooden xylophones, called timbila, fitted with gourd resonators.

MRT.text: Banc d'Arguin National Park mixes desert dunes and shallow sea along the Atlantic. Many migrating birds spend the winter there.

MUS.text: In Mauritius, about a quarter of the plants and animals live only on the island. The Black River Gorges protect the last fragments of its original forest.

MWI.text: Lake Malawi is home to over 350 species of small colourful fish called mbuna, almost all found nowhere else in the world.

NAM.text: In Namibia, the engravings at Twyfelfontein show rhinoceroses and giraffes. They record hunter-gatherer rituals going back at least 2,000 years.

NER.text: The Aïr and Ténéré reserves cover about 7.7 million hectares. They include the volcanic Aïr massif, a small Sahelian pocket in the Saharan desert.

NGA.text: Near Osogbo, the Osun Sacred Grove is one of the last remnants of primary forest in southern Nigeria. It holds sanctuaries, sculptures and artworks.

RWA.text: In Rwanda, Nyungwe mountain forest shelters one-fifth of Africa's primate species, including chimpanzees, and over 300 bird species.

SDN.text: Between the Nile and the Atbara, Meroe was the heartland of the Kingdom of Kush. Its remains include pyramids, temples and major water-management works.

SEN.text: In the Senegal River delta, the Djoudj sanctuary shelters some 1.5 million birds, such as white pelicans, purple herons and African spoonbills.

SLE.text: The name Sierra Leone comes from the Portuguese Serra Lyoa, "Lion Mountains", given by an explorer to the hills around Freetown harbour.

SOM.text: Somalia is the easternmost country of Africa, on the Horn of Africa. The frankincense tree (Boswellia) grows in its northern mountains.

SSD.text: In South Sudan, an estimated six million antelope and gazelles (white-eared kob, tiang, Mongalla gazelle) migrate across floodplains and savannas each year.

STP.text: São Tomé and Príncipe is a country of volcanic islands on the Equator. Its highest point, São Tomé Peak, rises to 2,024 m.

SWZ.text: At Ngwenya in Eswatini, people were already mining red ochre and sparkling haematite at least 42,000 years ago: one of the oldest mines in the world.

SYC.text: In Seychelles, on Praslin island, the Vallée de Mai is home to the coco de mer, whose seed is the largest in the plant kingdom.

TCD.text: In north-eastern Chad, in the Sahara desert, the Lakes of Ounianga form 18 connected lakes fed by groundwater.

TGO.text: In Koutammakou, in north-eastern Togo, the Batammariba build mud tower-houses called takienta, grouped in villages with springs and ceremonial spaces.

TUN.text: Dougga, built on a height overlooking a fertile plain, was the capital of a Libyco-Punic state. Its impressive Roman ruins can still be visited.

TZA.text: Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania rises to 5,895 m: the highest point in Africa, an isolated volcano whose snowy peak towers over the savannah.

UGA.text: In Uganda, Bwindi forest is home to almost half of the world's mountain gorillas, as well as over 200 tree species.

ZAF.text: In South Africa, the Vredefort Dome is the scar of a meteorite impact about 2 billion years old, one of the oldest and largest known on Earth.

ZMB.text: In Zambia, at Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya), the Zambezi, over 2 km wide, plunges into basalt gorges. Its mist can be seen from more than 20 km away.

ZWE.text: In Zimbabwe, the stone city of Great Zimbabwe, built between 1100 and 1450, gave the country its name: in Shona, "zimbabwe" means "house of stone".
